options.text: Twelve lunar months total about 354 days, which is shorter than the roughly 365-day seasonal year, so the lunar months drift through the seasons.
A purely lunar calendar stays locked to the seasons because Moon phases and seasons take equal times.
The seasons themselves become a little longer each year, so the lunar months can no longer keep pace with them.
Any school calendar that names months, even one not based on Moon phases, must drift from the seasons the same way.

stem:
Mehak's school fixes its annual day to one month on a purely lunar calendar. Each lunar month begins with a new Moon. Twelve lunar months make about 354 days, while seasons on Earth repeat in about 365 days. After several years the same annual day falls in a different season than it did at first.

Why does a purely lunar calendar not keep the same months aligned with the same seasons year after year?

teacher.key_rationale: A lunar year of about 354 days is shorter than the seasonal year of about 365 days, so lunar months drift relative to seasons. Claiming lock-step equality, blaming seasons for lengthening, or applying the rule to any named-month calendar miss the hinge.
